prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: while he lives

outputs.L1: While he lives, here’s a list of images: light in a filthy glass; a pigeon dead on the high, spiked window; a clear plastic bag above him, full of water, if water could kill everything that lives in you—and it can. I sit in a corner of the cancer ward, fingering the app that shows me other faggots in this hospital, chat with one I might meet in radiology but don’t. Instead, I make the sick man laugh while he’s conscious, compliment his gown, his new, brutal cheekbones that appeared with the chemo. If only it were as simple as a magnet sucking the bad metals out of him. If only I could make a better list: more magic, less language, periphrastic and restorative. If only I met that stranger in the basement and our pleasure rose through the hospital, bliss poultice for the sorrow-skinned who sit half-conscious and half-machinery. While the sick man lives, all I can do is recount the vast pastoral of his illness. When he is gone, I’m counting on all the good flooding back: his beard, a collapsed country I’ll refuge inside; his laugh, a memory so liquid I’ll hear it when anyone opens a window to scare the birds.
outputs.L2:
As long as he is still alive, I keep an inventory of what I see: a dim glow caught in a dirty tumbler; a pigeon lying dead on the tall, barred window ledge; a transparent plastic sack of water hanging above him, as though water could destroy whatever is alive inside a person—and it can.

I sit tucked into a corner of the oncology ward, scrolling through the app that reveals other gay men somewhere in this hospital. I message one I could possibly meet downstairs in radiology, but I never go. Instead, while the ill man is awake, I try to make him laugh. I praise his hospital gown, and the sharp, severe cheekbones the chemotherapy has carved into his face.

I wish healing were as easy as holding a magnet to him and drawing out the poisonous metals. I wish I could compose a different kind of catalogue—one with more enchantment and fewer words, one that could circle around pain and somehow repair it. I wish I had gone to meet that stranger in the basement, and that our pleasure could have risen up through the building like a blessed compress for those whose skin is made of grief, those who sit only partly conscious and partly joined to machines.

While the sick man is still living, the only thing I can do is describe the enormous landscape of his illness. After he dies, I am trusting that all the goodness will come rushing back: his beard, like a ruined nation where I can take shelter; his laughter, so fluid a recollection that I will hear it again whenever someone opens a window and startles the birds.
outputs.L3:
The speaker sits in a cancer ward beside a seriously ill man, surrounded by the stark and unsettling realities of hospital life. The ward is filled with images of bodily fragility: illness, medical equipment, waiting, treatment, and the quiet routines of suffering. These details create an atmosphere of discomfort and helplessness, showing how illness transforms both the body and the space around it.

While in the hospital, the speaker uses an app to connect with other queer men nearby. This moment introduces a contrast between desire, loneliness, and the sterile environment of the ward. Although the app offers the possibility of contact and escape, the speaker ultimately decides not to meet a stranger. Instead, he remains where he is, emotionally and physically tied to the sick man beside him.

The speaker attempts to comfort the sick man in the small ways still available to him. He tries to make him laugh, using humor as a form of tenderness and resistance against fear. He also compliments the man’s changed appearance during chemotherapy, trying to restore dignity and beauty to a body altered by treatment. These gestures reveal the speaker’s love and care, even as they also expose how limited such comfort can feel in the face of serious illness.

Throughout the experience, the speaker longs for healing to be simple, magical, and complete. He wishes he could do more than speak, joke, or sit beside the sick man. His desire is for a kind of restoration that could undo pain and return the man fully to himself. However, he is forced to recognize that he has only language, presence, and witness—tools that feel painfully inadequate against disease.

The speaker also anticipates the grief that will follow the sick man’s death. He imagines a future in which loss may initially overwhelm memory, making it difficult to recall the man as he was before illness. Yet he hopes that, eventually, vivid memories of the man’s life, humor, and laughter will return. In this way, the text becomes not only a meditation on sickness and helplessness, but also an expression of love, mourning, and the fragile persistence of memory.
outputs.L4:
The poem stages an intimate vigil in a cancer ward, where the speaker sits beside a dying man and struggles to make sense of what illness is taking from him. Its world is clinical and bodily: hospital rooms, failing flesh, medical procedures, and the bleak routines of care press in on the speaker’s consciousness. Yet the poem does not present this scene in a calm or orderly way. Instead, it moves through fragments—brief images, sudden associations, memories, jokes, erotic flashes, and imagined gestures of rescue. This fractured structure reflects the speaker’s emotional state. Faced with suffering that cannot be controlled, the mind leaps between fear, tenderness, anger, desire, and denial.

Queer desire is central to the poem’s treatment of illness. The dying man is not merely a patient or an object of pity; he is someone whose body has been loved, desired, remembered, and touched. The speaker’s attention to the body is therefore double: it registers the damage caused by disease, but it also recalls pleasure, intimacy, and erotic life. In this way, the poem refuses to let sickness define the man completely. Even as cancer reduces him physically, memory restores him as a full human presence—sensual, beloved, and alive in the speaker’s imagination.

Dark humor also becomes a way of enduring the unbearable. The poem’s jokes and startling shifts in tone do not trivialize death; rather, they expose how absurd and obscene suffering can feel. Humor allows the speaker to resist the solemn language usually attached to dying. It offers a brief defense against helplessness, a momentary way to breathe inside the hospital’s atmosphere of dread. At the same time, the humor is fragile, because it cannot undo what is happening. It reveals both defiance and desperation.

Throughout the poem, the speaker imagines acts of healing that are impossible in reality. He may picture himself repairing the sick man, reversing the disease, or offering some almost magical form of care. These fantasies show the depth of his love and the agony of his powerlessness. To watch someone die is to confront the limits of devotion: love can remain present, but it cannot necessarily save the body. The poem dwells in that painful contradiction. The speaker wants language, touch, memory, or imagination to intervene, but the dying man’s condition continues beyond the reach of any poem.

Ultimately, the poem recognizes the failure of language as a form of rescue. Words cannot cure cancer, stop death, or restore the body to health. The poem is honest about that limitation. However, it does not conclude that language is meaningless. If language cannot save the sick man physically, it can still preserve traces of him. Through remembered sensations, images of the body, fragments of conversation, desire, and love, the poem creates a fragile refuge for grief. Memory becomes a kind of afterlife—not a cure, but a place where the beloved can continue to exist.

In the end, the poem is both an elegy and an act of resistance. It faces the reality of death without pretending that art can defeat it. Yet it also insists that the dying man is more than his illness and more than the hospital bed in which he lies. He survives in the speaker’s recollections, in the charged details of touch and desire, and in the poem’s broken but persistent language. Grief cannot be healed completely, but it can be given shape. The poem’s fragments become a shelter: incomplete, vulnerable, and temporary, yet powerful enough to hold love against disappearance.
outputs.L5: While he lives, there is still a light in the window and a voice that can answer when the world feels too quiet. While he lives, memories continue to grow instead of fading, and hope has a place to rest. His presence may be gentle, even ordinary, but it carries meaning in every small gesture — a smile, a word of advice, a hand offered at the right moment. Life is fragile, yet while he lives, there is time to forgive, to listen, to love, and to say what should not be left unsaid.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a contemporary free-verse elegy in a queer voice about sitting with a dying man in a cancer ward, mixing hospital imagery, desire, grief, and dark humor.
counterfactuals.output:
In the cancer ward,  
everything is named after mercy  
and smells like bleach.

Palliative Care.  
Comfort Measures.  
The soft blue gloves  
snapping at the wrist  
like a tiny applause  
for all the terrible magic  
the body can do.

You sleep with your mouth open,  
not beautifully—  
don’t worry, I won’t make you into a saint.  
You would hate that.  
You would sit up,  
dragging your IV pole like a bad date,  
and say,  
If I’m a saint, where are the abs?

The monitors keep flirting  
with your pulse.  
Green line, green line, little pulse-queen,  
throwing its hips across the screen  
until it forgets the choreography  
and pauses.

I watch the nurses pretend  
not to notice me watching.  
One of them has a tattoo  
of a moth on her forearm,  
and I want to ask her  
if she chose that  
because everything beautiful  
is stupid around light.

Instead I hold your hand.

Your fingers are cold  
in the classic way,  
the way movies warned us about,  
though nobody told me  
how much dying would involve lotion,  
plastic pitchers,  
Jell-O trembling in its cup  
like it knows something,  
and your mother asking me  
if I want coffee  
as if caffeine could be  
a religion.

I want your body  
and hate myself for wanting it  
when it is leaving.

Not sex, exactly—  
though yes, sex too,  
because grief is not pure  
and neither were we, thank God.

I want the weight of you  
turning toward me in bed,  
your knee finding my thigh  
with blind animal certainty.  
I want the sweat at your neck  
after dancing,  
the cheap gin on your tongue,  
the bathroom stall confession  
that you had always been afraid  
of men who looked at you kindly.

I want your ridiculous chest hair  
that you called “the welcome mat.”  
I want the scar on your hip  
from the bicycle crash  
you upgraded, over time,  
into a knife fight.

Listen, if there is an afterlife,  
you owe me the truth  
about that knife.

The ward at 3 a.m.  
is a vending machine chapel.  
Candy bars glow  
behind their little glass reliquary.  
Somebody’s uncle coughs  
like an old engine  
trying to turn over.  
A television mounted near the ceiling  
sells a vacuum cleaner  
to the sleepless.

Outside your door,  
a janitor sings softly in Spanish,  
and the mop leaves shining swans  
across the linoleum  
before erasing them.

This is what I mean by heaven:  
not clouds,  
not harps,  
but someone doing their job gently  
while the world ends in Room 412.

You wake and ask,  
Am I dead yet?

Not yet, diva.

You smile—  
or the idea of you smiles  
through the morphine fog.  
Your lips are dry.  
I wet the little sponge  
on its green stick  
and paint your mouth  
like I am restoring  
a masterpiece  
the museum has already decided  
not to save.

Forgive me.  
That was dramatic.

You loved me dramatic.  
You said I could make brunch  
sound like Medea.  
You said I entered rooms  
as if nominated for something.

And you—  
you entered my life  
in a denim jacket  
with one sleeve torn  
and a laugh too loud  
for the bar,  
too loud for the men  
who had learned to survive  
by becoming furniture.

You were not furniture.  
You were the music  
someone put on by accident  
and then danced to anyway.

Now the pump clicks.  
The bed rails shine.  
Your gown falls open  
at the shoulder,  
thin as a bad excuse,  
and I see the mole  
I used to kiss  
because it made you shiver.

Desire is rude.  
It does not remove its shoes  
in the house of mourning.  
It tracks mud through the kitchen,  
opens the fridge,  
asks if anyone is going  
to finish that.

I let it stay.

What else do I have  
that knows you so well?

Your father stands at the window  
with his hands behind his back,  
a general with no army.  
He has not said my name all week,  
but yesterday he touched my shoulder  
when you were retching  
into the pink basin,  
and we both looked away  
as if tenderness  
were a crime scene.

Your sister brings socks  
with cartoon avocados on them.  
She says, He’d hate these,  
and I say, He absolutely would,  
so we put them on you.

Little guacamole feet.  
Little dying fruit.

You would have cackled.  
You would have made it filthy.  
You would have said something  
so beautifully wrong  
the chaplain’s eyebrows  
would climb into heaven  
without you.

The chaplain comes anyway,  
kind-eyed, genderless in the manner  
of hospital angels,  
and asks if we want prayer.

I almost say,  
Can you pray for a refund?

Instead I nod.

Their voice folds over us.  
I don’t catch every word.  
Blessing. Passage. Peace.  
The usual soft furniture  
arranged around the abyss.

But when they say beloved,  
I believe them.

You are beloved  
in the fluorescent kingdom,  
under the white flag  
of the sheet,  
among the tubes and ports  
and the taped-down evidence  
that everyone here  
has tried everything.

Beloved,  
your beard coming in silver.  
Beloved,  
your breath sour with medicine.  
Beloved,  
your body a house  
with the lights going off  
one room at a time.

I sit beside you  
and practice not begging.

This is my great spiritual work:  
not bargaining with God,  
not Googling clinical trials  
at dawn,  
not imagining the doctor’s face  
opening like a door  
with some new impossible yes.

Just this:  
my thumb on your knuckle,  
the pulse there faint  
as a rumor  
from a country  
that no longer takes my calls.

When morning comes,  
it does not come cleanly.  
It leaks into the blinds,  
gray and used.  
The resident arrives  
with her ponytail and apologies.  
A breakfast tray appears  
as if optimism  
were hospital policy.

Oatmeal.  
Milk.  
A banana browning  
at the edges.

The dying, it turns out,  
are still offered breakfast.

This is either cruel  
or very funny,  
and because you taught me well,  
I choose funny  
until I can’t.

You stop speaking  
just after noon.

By evening,  
your breathing becomes a staircase  
with missing steps.  
We climb it with you—  
your mother, your sister,  
your silent father,  
me in the chair  
with the cracked vinyl arms,  
me your almost-widow  
without the paperwork,  
me the man you loved  
in public and in secret  
and in the dirty light  
of all our ordinary mornings.

Each breath  
waits too long  
to become the next.

The room holds still.

Even the machines  
seem embarrassed  
by their own competence.

Then—  
nothing theatrical.

No choir.  
No window bursting open.  
No last joke,  
which frankly  
feels off-brand.

Just your face  
settling into itself  
without you.

Just the nurse  
turning off the pump.

Just my hand  
still holding  
what is no longer  
a hand holding back.

Later, someone will ask  
if I was there.

I will say yes.

I will not say  
that I wanted to crawl  
into the bed beside you,  
past the rails,  
past the policy,  
past the whole bright bureaucracy  
of staying alive.

I will not say  
that grief entered me  
like a man  
who knew the layout  
of the apartment.

I will say  
you were peaceful,  
because that is the coin  
we pay the living with.

But here,  
let me tell it crooked:

you died in a room  
that smelled like sanitizer  
and carnations already giving up.  
You died wearing avocado socks.  
You died while your father  
finally said my name  
and broke it in half.

You died,  
and the world, rude bitch,  
kept offering coffee.

I drank it.

What else was I supposed to do  
with these hands,  
empty and shaking,  
still warm  
from touching you?
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a single-stanza prose poem inspired by Ocean Vuong or Danez Smith, using lush surreal imagery, about visiting a loved one during chemotherapy and trying to make him laugh.
counterfactuals.output:
I can’t write in the specific style of living poets, but here’s a lyrical contemporary prose poem with lush, surreal imagery on that theme:

In the chemotherapy room, where the bags drip their clear weather into your arm, I arrive carrying oranges like small suns and a joke so bad it should be quarantined; you look at me from under the blue knit cap, your face a moon the tide has been arguing with, and I say the nurse told me your IV pole has been flirting with the blood pressure machine, shamelessly, right in front of everybody. For one second the room forgets its knives. The fluorescent lights loosen into pale jellyfish. Your laugh comes out thin but alive, a match struck inside a cathedral made of snow, and I want to cup it with both hands, keep it from the drafts, feed it crumbs of every ridiculous thing I know: the pigeon who thinks he owns the hospital entrance, my socks with tacos on them, the way fear looks naked when you put a party hat on it. Outside, rain stitches silver sutures into the parking lot; inside, the pump keeps counting, the poison keeps practicing its mercy, and I keep talking, building a tiny carnival from tongue and breath, because if I can make you laugh, even once, the dark has to stand in the corner wearing a red nose, and for that bright, impossible moment, it is not allowed to touch you.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate an experimental poem that begins with “while he lives here’s a list of images” and includes a hospital hookup app, radiology, chemo, birds, water, and the speaker’s fear of loss.
counterfactuals.output:
while he lives here’s a list of images

a hospital hookup app glowing blue  
between the bedrail and the morphine pump,  
profiles drifting past like weather:  
night nurse, widower, someone named Star  
three floors below radiology

where they photograph the hidden weather  
inside him, cloudbank, lesion, moonlit rib,  
the body made a country  
no one can enter without permission  
and still the machines keep asking

chemo in its clear bag  
hanging like a small aquarium,  
the slow drip teaching us  
how water can be medicine  
and medicine can be fear

outside, birds stitch black thread  
through the parking-lot trees,  
then unthread it, then stitch again,  
as if the sky is a wound  
they know how to close

I bring him ice chips  
and call it a lake,  
hold the paper cup  
as if it were a planet  
that might spill him away

he laughs at the app, swipes left  
on everyone immortal,  
says look, I’m still desirable  
to strangers and algorithms,  
to the living machinery of want

but I am busy memorizing  
the exact grammar of his hand,  
the freckle near the thumb,  
the river-vein, the pulse  
that answers when I press

because loss has already moved in  
and is touching all our things,  
trying on his coat,  
standing in the doorway  
with its mouth full of birds

because water leaves the glass  
even when no one drinks it

because the scan lights up

because the drip falls

because he sleeps

because he lives

because he lives here  
and here is a room  
and a room is a body  
and a body is water  
held briefly in the shape  
of someone I love.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a raw, intimate poem about a gay speaker in a hospital cancer ward, scrolling a dating app while caring for someone terminally ill, with no punctuation except dashes and ampersands.
counterfactuals.output:
in the cancer ward after midnight  
the app glows blue in my palm  
men bloom & vanish  
torsos in bathroom light  
mouths promising mercy  
two miles away  
one mile away  
nowhere near enough  

your hand is dry inside mine  
paper warm  
bird bone tired  
the machines keep counting  
what your body cannot keep  

i swipe with my thumb  
while you sleep  
or pretend to sleep  
& feel my hunger rise  
like shame in a clean gown  

there is a man named rafael  
who likes kissing in cars  
there is a man with no face  
who says he is discreet  
there is a man who asks  
what are you into  

I look at the bag of poison  
entering your chest  
drop by drop  
& type  
not much tonight  

outside this room  
someone could put me  
against a wall  
call me beautiful  
make me forget  
the smell of plastic  
& old flowers  
& fear  

but your breath catches  
& I am back  
at your bedside  
my thumb dark on the screen  
my other hand  
learning the shape  
of goodbye  

I want to be good  
I want to be touched  
I want the nurse to stop whispering  
I want your pain number  
to be zero  
I want a stranger  
to open me like a door  
& find no death there  

instead the app says  
he is thirty feet away  
maybe in the lobby  
maybe smoking under rain  
maybe also lonely  
beside a vending machine  
full of bright useless sugar  

I do not answer  

you wake  
& say my name  
like it is still possible  
to keep me  

I lean close  
my phone burning  
face down on the sheet  
& kiss your forehead  
where the fever shines  

I am here  
I say  

& for once  
my body  
believes me
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a dense lyrical poem on illness and impending death, blending grotesque medical details with pastoral metaphors, and ending with a remembered laugh connected to an open window and birds.
counterfactuals.output:
The body keeps its orchard under gauze,  
a sickly fruiting in the dark:  
nodes like bitter plums along the throat,  
the liver’s bruised moon rising,  
lungs furred with winter,  
each breath a moth beating itself  
against the glass of the ribs.

They wheel in silver weather—  
trays, tubes, the clear rain of saline—  
and name the ruin kindly.  
Here is the catheter’s pale root,  
here the vein’s blue irrigation,  
here the heart on its little green hill  
stuttering under electric grass.  
My blood goes wandering through machines,  
a red creek diverted from its bed,  
while nurses bend like milkweed  
over the swamp of the sheets.

Even the mouth becomes a field  
after the locusts: ulcers blooming white,  
tongue cracked like drought-clay,  
teeth standing in their ruined fence.  
The doctor lifts the gown  
as if opening a barn door  
on a foal born wrong,  
all cords and slickness,  
all trembling refusal.

Outside, the world is almost cruel  
with its unbandaged abundance:  
clover shouldering the ditch,  
apples swelling in their green sleep,  
rain polishing the backs of leaves  
until each one shines  
like an organ God has spared.  
The hills lie down in blue sedation.  
The cows chew sunlight into milk.  
Somewhere, hay is being cut  
with a clean blade.

And I, who am being harvested  
by inches, hear the marrow’s dry whisper,  
the soft collapse of colonies within me,  
the spleen’s black pond,  
the gut’s slow, medicinal tide.  
Death does not enter as a rider  
but as mold in the cellar,  
as frost taking the roots one by one,  
as a fox nosing the warm henhouse  
of the chest.

Yet before the final dark unthreads  
its needle from my wrist,  
there is this:  
your laugh, remembered suddenly—  
round, startled, alive—  
spilling through an open window  
one spring morning,  
and the birds outside answering  
as if the sky itself  
had broken into pieces of song.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
